clinician.final_diagnosis: MFS-GBS overlap syndrome associated with the Oxford-AstraZeneca SARS-CoV2 vaccination
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 63-year-old man presented with acute onset severe bilateral facial weakness, unsteadiness, lower limb weakness, and paraesthesia 14 days following Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccination. Neurological examination revealed profound sensory ataxia, facial diplegia, proximal lower limb weakness, bilateral lower limb areflexia, and impaired distal lower limb proprioception. CSF analysis showed albuminocytological dissociation (markedly elevated protein of 2.99 g/L with low cell count). MRI of the brain demonstrated enhancement of the facial and oculomotor nerves bilaterally. Serum anti-GQ1b antibody was negative. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography showed evidence of a long-standing axonal neuropathy with no acute abnormalities. On the second day of admission, he developed diplopia and partial bilateral cranial nerve III palsies. He was treated with a 5-day course of intravenous immunoglobulin and supportive care, followed by 4 weeks of inpatient rehabilitation. At 6 weeks post-symptom onset, his ophthalmoplegia and ataxia resolved, with minimal residual bilateral facial weakness and persistent bilateral proximal lower limb weakness.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Acute onset severe bilateral facial weakness, unsteadiness, lower limb weakness and paraesthesia developed over 48 hours, 14 days post Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccination.

Neurological examination revealed profound sensory ataxia, facial diplegia involving the forehead, proximal lower limb weakness, bilateral lower limb areflexia and impaired distal lower limb proprioception.
CSF examination revealed albuminocytological dissociation with a markedly elevated protein of 2.99 g/L and low cell count (4 /µL lymphocytes, 1 /µL polymorphonuclear leukocytes).
MRI of the brain with contrast demonstrated enhancement of the facial and oculomotor nerves bilaterally, consistent with facial diplegia and partial bilateral cranial nerve III palsies.
Patient developed diplopia on lateral gaze bilaterally, impaired adduction, restricted upward gaze and intorsion with down gaze bilaterally, consistent with partial cranial nerve III palsies.
Patient was treated with a 5-day course of intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g/kg) and supportive care.
At 6 weeks after onset of symptoms, the patient’s ophthalmoplegia and ataxia have resolved and he has minimal residual bilateral facial weakness.
